title: Visualizing Your Data: Creating Effective Plots with ggplot2 in R
description:
Ever struggled to turn raw data into clear, compelling visuals? Whether you're presenting findings, exploring patterns, or just trying to make your data speak, effective visualization is key. In this workshop, you'll learn how to use ggplot2, a popular R package, to create publication-ready plots that reveal insights and tell stories.

This hands-on workshop introduces ggplot2, a powerful and flexible data visualization package in R based on the grammar of graphics. You’ll learn how to create and customize a variety of plot types—such as bar charts, scatter plots, histograms, and line graphs—while also learning how to choose the most appropriate visualization for different types of data. Whether you’re new to R or want to improve the way you communicate data, this session offers practical guidance and reusable code to get you started.

In this workshop, participants will learn to:

  • Describe the key components of the grammar of graphics used in ggplot2
  • Apply ggplot2 techniques to effectively communicate data insights in R
  • Create basic visualizations such as bar charts, scatter plots, histograms, and line graphs using ggplot2
  • Choose appropriate plot types for different kinds of data
  • Customize plots by modifying aesthetics, adding labels, adjusting color schemes, and applying themes

No prior experience with R Studio is required. This workshop is ideal for researchers who are looking to enhance their data storytelling skills through visualization.

title: Creating Documents with LaTeX
description:
This workshop will introduce you to LaTeX, a typesetting system commonly used in STEM disciplines to create high-quality documents and easily write mathematical equations. We will discuss tools for writing in LaTeX, the structural elements of LaTeX, text formatting, and commands for writing mathematical equations. Whether you are preparing academic assignments, research manuscripts, or technical documents, this session will provide a practical foundation for getting started with LaTeX.

This session is ideal for students, researchers, and instructors who are new to LaTeX and interested in creating professional-quality academic and technical documents. No prior experience with LaTeX is required.

By the end of this session, participants will be able to:

  1. Identify common tools and platforms for writing and compiling LaTeX documents.
  2. Explain the basic structure of a LaTeX document, including the preamble, document body, and sectional organization.
  3. Format text and organize content using core LaTeX commands.
  4. Create and customize common environments, including lists, figures, and equations.
  5. Write and format mathematical expressions within text and display equations using LaTeX syntax.
  6. Develop and compile a simple LaTeX document from start to finish.

title: DORA: Establishing & Maintaining Researcher Profiles
description:
The ability to effectively track and communicate your research impact is an essential skill for today’s researchers. Profile tools like ORCID, Google Scholar, and McMaster Experts provide valuable spaces to showcase your research outputs, from publications and datasets to creative works, while enabling efficient workflows for demonstrating your impact. This workshop will guide researchers through the process of creating and maintaining researcher profiles, from initial setup to streamlined upkeep and generating basic impact reports.

This workshop is part of the DORA (San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment) Workshop Series, which explores practical approaches for showcasing and evaluating research beyond traditional metrics. Together, these sessions focus on strengthening researcher visibility, communicating research impact, and recognizing the value of diverse scholarly contributions.

This session is ideal for researchers and graduate students interested in establishing an online presence, increasing the visibility of their work, and tracking the impact of their research.

By the end of this session, participants will be able to:

  1. Select the most appropriate research profile(s) for their needs.
  2. Automate the initial population and maintenance of their research profile(s).
  3. Generate basic research impact reports using profile data.

title: Introduction to Data Analysis with SPSS
description:
Looking for an accessible way to analyze data? SPSS is a widely used statistical software that makes it easy to explore, summarize, and interpret data—no programming required. This beginner-friendly workshop introduces SPSS through hands-on activities using its point-and-click interface. You’ll learn how to import data, run basic descriptive statistics, and perform simple analyses like t-tests and correlations.

This session is ideal for students, researchers, and staff who want a user-friendly introduction to statistical analysis. No prior experience required!

By the end of this session, participants will be able to:
1. Navigate the SPSS interface and load data
2. Run descriptive statistics such as means, frequencies, and standard deviations
3. Conduct basic statistical tests (e.g., t-tests, correlations)
4. Interpret and export results from SPSS

title: Topics, Methods, and Resources To "Do More with Digital Scholarship"
description:
Digital scholarship encompasses a wide range of approaches, tools, and methods that leverage digital technologies to support research, teaching, learning, knowledge mobilization, and creative practice. Join us for a 1-hour introductory session, where we’ll address some of your fundamental questions about Digital Scholarship, including: What is it? How can I integrate it into my learning, research, teaching, personal learning and professional development? What tools and services exist to help me learn more, get started, or engage more deeply? Participants will learn more about Digital Scholarship topics and methods, McMaster’s Lewis and Ruth Sherman Centre for Digital Scholarship (SCDS), and the many ways in which the SCDS can support their work.

This session is ideal for students, faculty, staff, and researchers who are new to digital scholarship or interested in learning more about digital tools, methods, and support services available at McMaster University. No prior experience is required.

By the end of this session, participants will be able to:

  1. Describe digital scholarship and the variety of topics and methods it encompasses.
  2. Explain how digital scholarship relates to and augments traditional disciplinary research and learning.
  3. Describe the role of the Sherman Centre for Digital Scholarship in supporting research, teaching, and personal development.
  4. Identify the digital scholarship tools, resources, and services that may be of relevance to your research, teaching, and personal development objectives.

title: Data Management Plan Bootcamp (In-Person)

description:

If you're in the process of creating a DMP, either for a grant application or for your own research, join RDM Services for this afternoon session. The RDM services team will provide tailored guidance as you write your plan on site, and we'll have some light snacks and refreshments to keep you going. Come away with a clear path forward or even a finished DMP!

This participatory session is especially relevant for researchers at all levels in the beginning stages of a research project or streamlining best practices for their research team. Come on your own, send your research staff, or bring your whole research group. Let us know if you're joining as a research team - we'll make sure you get a table to work together at!

title: Multivariable Analysis with R
description:
Interested in learning how to examine the relationship between multiple variables and an outcome of interest? Multivariable regression analysis is a foundational statistical technique that allows researchers to account for potential confounding factors, evaluate associations, and generate more robust evidence from their data. Through live demonstrations and hands-on exercises in R, participants will gain practical experience developing, evaluating, and interpreting multivariable regression models.

This workshop introduces the complete workflow for conducting multivariable analyses in R, from data preparation and model building to diagnostic testing and research reporting. Whether you are conducting quantitative research, analyzing observational data, or looking to strengthen your statistical skills, this session will provide a practical foundation for applying multivariable regression methods in a research context.

This session is ideal for researchers, graduate students, and analysts seeking to strengthen their quantitative research skills. Basic familiarity with R and introductory statistical concepts is recommended.

By the end of this session, participants will be able to:

  1. Prepare and clean research datasets for multivariable analysis in R.
  2. Fit and interpret multivariable linear and logistic regression models.
  3. Assess model assumptions and diagnose common analytical issues.
  4. Select appropriate variables and develop multivariable models using practical modeling strategies.

title: DORA: Tracking the Impact of Non-Traditional Research Outputs
description:
From datasets and code to podcasts, reports, and performances, not all research outputs take the form of journal articles or books. These are known as Non-Traditional Research Outputs (NTROs): scholarly or creative works that fall outside conventional academic publishing. While NTROs make up a significant and growing part of research activity, they are often under-recognized in systems that track and assess research impact. In this workshop, participants will explore current best practices for tracking and communicating the impact of NTROs and learn how these practices align with movements such as the San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment (DORA), which advocates for more responsible and inclusive approaches to research assessment.

This workshop is part of the DORA (San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment) Workshop Series, which explores practical approaches for showcasing and evaluating research beyond traditional metrics. Together, these sessions focus on strengthening researcher visibility, communicating research impact, and recognizing the value of diverse scholarly contributions.

This session is ideal for researchers, creators, and academic staff working with non-traditional outputs who want to make their work more visible, trackable, and valued.

By the end of this session, participants will be able to:

  1. Create persistent identifiers (e.g., DOIs) and metadata records for NTROs.
  2. Incorporate NTROs into existing researcher profile systems (e.g., ORCID and McMaster Experts).
  3. Identify strategies for increasing the visibility, discoverability, and impact of NTROs.
  4. Communicate the value of NTROs within responsible research assessment frameworks.

title: Creating Small and Ugly Open Educational Resource (OER)
description:

This workshop will focus on taking the content you’ve already created and turning it into an open educational resource (OER), without a lot of time or effort. We’ll discuss strategies for publishing and sharing educational content such as lecture notes, slide decks, assessments, or multimedia. We’ll find simple ways to openly share educational resources so that others can access, share, and adapt them. We’ll focus on expanding access to educational materials, with one small, ugly step at a time.

This session is ideal for instructors, teaching assistants, educational developers, librarians, and anyone interested in sharing educational materials more openly. No prior experience with OER creation or open licensing is required.

By the end of this session, participants will be able to:

  1. Explain what is meant by “open educational resources”
  2. Select an appropriate open license for a resource they might share

title: Exploring Statistics Canada Data Resources
description:
Statistics Canada provides access to a rich collection of data resources that support research, teaching, policy development, and evidence-based decision-making. From Census data and national surveys to public use microdata files and geographic datasets, these resources offer valuable insights into Canada's population, economy, health, and society. Through guided demonstrations, participants will learn how to navigate Statistics Canada's online platforms, locate relevant datasets, and understand the different types of statistical products available for analysis.

This workshop introduces the core data products and tools offered by Statistics Canada, while also highlighting library-supported resources that expand access to Canadian data. Whether you are beginning a research project, looking for data to support coursework, or seeking reliable Canadian statistics, this session will provide a practical foundation for finding, accessing, and working with Statistics Canada data.

This session is ideal for students, faculty, staff, and researchers who are new to Statistics Canada data resources or looking to strengthen their data discovery skills. No prior experience with Statistics Canada datasets is required.

By the end of this session, participants will be able to:

  1. Identify the major data products and resources available through Statistics Canada.
  2. Navigate the Statistics Canada website to find Census data, survey data, data tables, and analytical reports.
  3. Distinguish between different types of Statistics Canada data products, including aggregate tables, Public Use Microdata Files (PUMFs), and geographic data.
  4. Search for and retrieve relevant Canadian statistical data for research, teaching, and coursework.
  5. Interpret basic dataset documentation, metadata, and methodological information.
  6. Access library-supported data resources and services, including CHASS, ODESI, and data consultation support.
  7. Apply appropriate citation practices when using Statistics Canada data in academic and research outputs.

title: Social Media Scraping and Analysis with Zeeschuimer and 4Cat
description:
The landscape of social media data collection has changed significantly in recent years, creating new challenges and opportunities for researchers interested in studying online platforms. This workshop introduces Zeeschuimer and 4CAT, a powerful combination of browser-based and server-based tools designed to support the collection, management, and analysis of data from selected social media platforms. Through guided demonstrations, participants will learn how these tools can be used to support digital and computational research while navigating the evolving social media research environment.

This session is ideal for students, researchers, and instructors interested in social media research, digital methods, and computational approaches to studying online platforms. No prior experience with web scraping or social media data analysis is required.

By the end of this session, participants will be able to:

  1. Explain the purpose and capabilities of the Zeeschuimer and 4CAT tools.
  2. Collect data from supported social media platforms using Zeeschuimer.
  3. Import, manage, and explore collected datasets within 4CAT.
  4. Conduct basic analyses of social media data using 4CAT's built-in tools and workflows.
  5. Identify ethical, legal, and methodological considerations related to social media data collection and analysis

title: Getting More Out of LaTeX: Citations, Presentations, and Dissertations
description:
Have you already learned how to create a LaTeX document? Do you already know how to write out beautiful mathematical notation using slash codes? How to insert all the images and table you could ever dream of? And you still want to learn how to get more out of LaTeX? Then this workshop is for you! Learn how LaTeX handles citations, from using .bib files and changing citation styles to integrating the Zotero citation manager with Overleaf. We’ll also show you how to create a conference-ready presentation deck without leaving your LaTeX editor. In addition, we'll explore how to use LaTeX templates for large writing projects such as theses and dissertations.

This session is ideal for students, researchers, and instructors who have prior experience creating and editing basic LaTeX documents and are looking to expand their skills for academic writing, presentations, and long-form projects. Familiarity with LaTeX fundamentals is recommended.

By the end of this session, participants will be able to:

  1. Use .bib files to display citations in multiple styles in LaTeX documents
  2. Connect Zotero to Overleaf and add a citation to their document
  3. Create a slide deck using the Beamer LaTeX plugin
  4. Understand how to use a LaTeX template for a large writing project like a dissertation or thesis

title: Simple Sabotage: A Field Manual for Refusing Corporate AI
location: Sherman Centre for Digital Scholarship (1st Floor, Mills Library)
description:
Simple Sabotage was a document written by the US Office of Strategic Services in 1944 to train everyday citizens to thwart the forces of fascism (a resource garnering renewed attention in this particular political moment). This quick fix workshop is a tongue-in-cheek update to train citizen-saboteurs to thwart the predetermined inevitability of corporate AI from micro to the macro: a history of GenAI, opportunities for data liberation, local LLMs, resisting corporate software by switching to Linux, everyday data privacy practices like turning of Connected Experiences in M365, and more. We'll explore tangible everyday practices to motivate the saboteur (you!) and provide them with specific suggestions for tools, targets, timing to resist and re-imagine AI futures.

No experience except your lived experience is necessary. While we aren't all against all AI, understanding how it works and making intentional decisions about how, when, and whose data is used is increasingly important. Join us to talk tactics!

By the end of this session, participants will be able to:

  1. Describe the history of GenAI and how it works
  2. Identify potential sources for data liberation
  3. Choose alternative platforms or configure settings to protect your privacy
  4. Propose possible pathways to re-imagine AI futures.

title: Prediction Model Performance for Binary Outcomes in R
description:
Interested in learning how to evaluate the performance and reliability of prediction models? Assessing model performance is a critical step in determining whether a prediction model is accurate, trustworthy, and suitable for research or clinical applications. Through live demonstrations and hands-on exercises in R, participants will gain practical experience using widely accepted methods to evaluate binary outcome prediction models. This workshop introduces key concepts and techniques for assessing prediction model performance, including discrimination, calibration, and internal validation. Participants will learn how to generate and interpret common performance metrics and create clear, publication-ready visualizations to communicate their findings effectively.

This session is ideal for researchers, graduate students, and analysts interested in developing and evaluating prediction models. Basic familiarity with R and regression modeling concepts is recommended.

By the end of this session, participants will be able to:

  1. Develop prediction models for binary outcomes and generate predicted probabilities in R.
  2. Assess model discrimination using the C-statistic (AUC) and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves.
  3. Evaluate model calibration using calibration plots and calibration statistics.
  4. Perform internal validation using resampling techniques such as bootstrapping and cross-validation.
  5. Create publication-ready figures, tables, and summaries to effectively communicate prediction model performance.

title: Setting up a New Reproducible Research Project: Data Sharing, Documentation, File Formats, and More!
description:
Reproducible research means setting things up so that after a late-night moonlight and caffeine powered deep work breakthrough you can wake up the next morning and know what you did and explain it to your supervisor. title: Data Deposit and Retention: Get Readier for Requirements from Funders and Publishers
description:
Are looming requirements for data retention, deposit, and availability getting you down? Or maybe a journal is asking you to deposit your research data and you don't know where to start? Get readier for requirements with this quick, timely webinar.

Data deposit and data sharing are increasingly recognized as best practices to support open research, reproducibility, research integrity, collaboration, and more. In January 2027, the Tri-Agencies (CIHR, NSERC, and SSHRC) are targeted to implement a data deposit and retention requirement for funded projects. Many journals are also asking researchers to share or make data available: BMJ, PLOS, Nature, NEJM, and Frontiers. But what's the best repository to share it in? How do you meet this requirement if you have sensitive or very large datasets?

If you're a researcher, on a research team, a research support staff, or a student with questions about impending requirements, this session is for you. It's also appropriate to bring anyone up to speed on long-term data management for a publication, grant, or project.

By the end of this session, participants will be able to:

  1. Bullet-point their responsibilities under the Tri-Agencies' impending data deposit, availability, and retention requirements
  2. Locate an appropriate repository for their dataset.
  3. Find RDM consultations and other resources to help them meet requirements.
  4. Outline tools to support documentation and metadata best practices, including READMEs, codebooks, and data dictionaries.

description:

How do you know when you're working with Personal Health Information or just health research data? Should you store data at the university or the hospital?

We’ll talk about data storage, data sharing in a team and managing access, data sharing and deposit to support long-term retention, and more! title: Survival Analysis with R
description:
Many research questions in health, clinical, and epidemiological research focus not only on whether an event occurs, but also on when it occurs. Survival analysis provides a powerful set of statistical techniques for examining time-to-event outcomes such as mortality, disease recurrence, hospitalization, or recovery. Through live demonstrations and hands-on exercises in R, participants will gain practical experience analyzing and interpreting survival data using widely used survival analysis methods. This workshop introduces the fundamentals of survival analysis, including Kaplan-Meier survival curves, log-rank tests, and Cox proportional hazards regression. Participants will learn how to prepare time-to-event data, compare survival experiences across groups, and model factors associated with survival outcomes. Whether you are conducting clinical, epidemiological, or health services research, this session will provide a practical foundation for applying survival analysis techniques in R.

This session is ideal for researchers, graduate students, and analysts working with time-to-event data. Basic familiarity with R and introductory statistical concepts is recommended.

By the end of this session, participants will be able to:

  1. Prepare and manage time-to-event data for survival analysis in R.
  2. Estimate and interpret Kaplan-Meier survival curves.
  3. Compare survival distributions between groups using the log-rank test.
  4. Fit and interpret Cox proportional hazards regression models.
  5. Assess the proportional hazards assumption and perform model diagnostics.
  6. Create publication-ready tables, figures, and summaries to communicate survival analysis results effectively.

title: Abducted by Aliens? 🛸 Building Sustainable File, Folder & Documentation Workflows
description:
You arrive at work to see your project's primary investigator/research coordinator/key graduate student disappearing into a UFO's buzzing blue beam; with all their project knowledge and disconnected laptop gone forever…or at least til the aliens return them home. While an alien abduction is unlikely to strike your research team, life happens: research coordinators get hired into roles at another university, graduate students return home, PIs go on research leave or get sick unexpectedly and need to step back. Clearly writing out research processes, clear file and folder workflows, organized data storage systems, and more are excellent research practices to make sure everyone is on the same page and your research project is resilient to change. It can also help keep qualitative coding and variables or units of measurement in quantitative projects consistent across multiple researchers. Even if you're going solo as a graduate student, documenting your data and keeping a good research log will help you unpack what you did when it comes time to write up your project.

No prior knowledge is required! This session is designed for researchers who want to think through their documentation and workflows; from graduate students working alone to tenured faculty with a huge research team. Undergraduate students interested in future research might also find it interesting.

By the end of this session, participants will be able to:

  1. Create quality file names from bad ones
  2. Design folder structures that make sense for their project
  3. Identify types of documentation and locate templates and resources to help them create their own
  4. Transfer knowledge of storage workflows into their own projects

title: Data Feminism: Power, Inequality, and Social Change
location: Sherman Centre for Digital Scholarship (1st Floor, Mills Library)
description:
Who gets counted, who gets excluded, and who benefits from the stories data tells?

In this workshop, participants will be introduced to Data Feminism, which Catherine D'Ignazio and Lauren Klein describe as "a way of thinking about data, both their uses and their limits, that is informed by direct experience, by a commitment to action, and by intersectional feminist thought" (2020). Together, we will explore how data practices can reproduce inequalities related to gender, race, sexuality, disability, class, age, geography, and other intersecting systems of power, as well as how data can be used to make those inequities visible, challenge unequal distributions of power, and support social change. Tying an understanding of inequality to a commitment to action, we will introduce data practices that can help make equality a reality, including Mel Mikhail's proposals for data management in feminist research projects. Through an introduction to the principles of Data Feminism, participants will reflect on how these ideas can inform their own research, teaching, community engagement, and advocacy efforts.

New to Data Feminism? No problem! This workshop is designed for anyone interested in learning how data can be used to challenge inequities and support social change. Researchers, educators, students, librarians, staff, and community members are all welcome.

By the end of this session, participants will be able to:

  1. Describe key principles of Data Feminism.
  2. Explain how systems of power shape data collection, interpretation, and use.
  3. Identify opportunities to use data to amplify marginalized perspectives and advance social change.
  4. Reflect on their own data types and what kinds of biases and ideological beliefs inform them.

description:

description:

The Responsible AI for Digital Humanities Projects workshop combines critical questioning with hands-on practice to explore whether and potentially how AI should be used for DH research. We will discuss justice-oriented AI initiatives, resources to help reimagine / reclaim / refuse AI, and a survey of ways digital humanists are working with AI. Throughout the workshop, running open source models on your own machine rather than relying on frontier models and other sustainable practices such as scaling (down) to the needs of your project will be emphasized. By the end of this session, participants will be able to:

  2. Plan a DH project that considers and minimizes potential harms when using AI methods.
  3. Run open source models on your own computer to evaluate suitability and conduct DH research.
  4. Discuss AI requirements for your DH project capably with collaborators and on grant applications.

location: Sherman Centre for Digital Scholarship (1st Floor, Mills Library)
description:
Everyone talks about the weather, but have you ever thought about measuring it? From community crowdsourcing applications to projects around the house to more rigorous research applications, low-cost weather stations can be valuable monitoring tools and a source of personal learning and enjoyment. In this full-day, hands-on and in-person bootcamp, you will learn how to build and program simple circuits that connect a microcontroller (Arduino) to a suite of environmental sensors (temperature, humidity, light intensity, etc.) to make a working weather station. In the second half of this session, you'll learn the basics of 3D model design and development to create a 3D-printable model of an enclosure for your station.

No prior experience with electronics or 3D model development is required, as we'll start at the basics!

By the end of this session, participants will be able to:

  1. Describe the fundamental concepts and operational principles of simple circuits, sensors and actuators.
  2. Apply fundamental principles to build simple circuits that interact with their surrounding environments.
  3. Create and modify software code to control the device and create comments to document its functionality.
  4. Explain the basics of temperature measurement and the considerations necessary to do it with accuracy and consistency.
  5. Discuss the basic principles of 3D model design and development.

title: Field Recording: Capturing Audio for Podcasting, Qualitative Research, Environmental Science, Art, Music, and More!
location: Sherman Centre for Digital Scholarship (1st Floor, Mills Library)
description:
Do you want to get outside for your interviews and focus groups, ecological study, or creative practice? While some interviews are best held indoors in a studio like those at Lyons New Media Centre, there are a million reason to leave the recording studio behind. This can include capturing natural or ambient sounds, making a podcast richer with audio from daily life, or going to an interview subject's home turf so they feel a bit more comfortable. This 3-hour intensive will give you hands-on experience with field recording for a range of purposes.

A trifecta of experts will boost your technical and creative decision-making:

  • Sam Hansen brings experience field recording for their podcast productions, working with the BBC, NPR, CBC on tape syncs, and setting up mics outside the studio.
  • Lyons' own Carlie King will introduce you to their field recording equipment kits (with H6 and H4 zoom recorders) and share details on microphone recording patterns.
  • Danica Evering will give practical overview of approaches to recording with future editing and artistic choices in mind.

This session is designed for absolute beginners who have no experience with field recording but we also welcome audio enthusiasts who want to find community. We will intentionally keep this very interdisciplinary to reach anyone looking to record audio: from Health Sciences researchers recording interviews in busy clinical settings to ecologists and biologists looking to study bioacoustics of bird song to iArts (Integrated Arts) undergrads working on a multimedia project. Come record with us!

By the end of this session, participants will be able to:

  1. Record intentional audio outdoors and in unconventional indoor environments.
  2. Select appropriate microphone and recording devices for their desired use case, as well as windscreens and other peripherals
  3. Locate campus resources for field recording
  4. Prepare to make creative decisions with field recordings

title: Data Management Plan Bootcamp (In-Person)
location: Sherman Centre for Digital Scholarship (1st Floor, Mills Library)
description:
Let us be your body double with this in-person bootcamp! Data Management Plans (DMPs) are both incredibly helpful research tools and increasingly required for grants but it can hard to know how to complete a Data Management Plan if it’s your first time. This session is carefully timed for researchers completing a CFI or Tri-Agency grant this fall. If you're in the process of creating a DMP, either for a grant application or for your own research, join RDM Services for this afternoon session. The RDM services team will provide tailored guidance as you write your plan on site, and we'll have some light snacks and refreshments to keep you going. Come away with a clear path forward or even a finished DMP!

This participatory session is especially relevant for researchers at all levels in the beginning stages of a research project or streamlining best practices for their research team. Come on your own, send your research staff, or bring your whole research group. Let us know if you're joining as a research team - we'll make sure you get a table to work together at!

By the end of this session, participants will be able to:

  1. Identify the 5 key components of a data management plan (DMP).
  2. Compare strong and weak responses in each section of a DMP.
  3. Develop a tailored outline, or potentially a complete draft, of their own DMP!

title: Qualitative Data Bootcamp: Clean Collection, De-identification, and Analysis Basics
location: Sherman Centre for Digital Scholarship (1st Floor, Mills Library)
description:
Want some focused skill development time for your qualitative practice? Get ready to take care of and analyze qualitative research data: interview transcripts, surveys oral histories, focus groups, field notes, artistic expression, photovoice and more. Qualitative methods let us understand lived experiences and motivations, see a research question from different standpoints, and highlight contexts.

This bootcamp is for those trying to get a qualitative research project off the ground who would like support on different aspects across the research lifecycle. Starting with Data Management Planning, we will discuss data management during collection, qualitative data analysis fundamentals such as conducting the analysis, and end with effective ways of sharing data and communicating results. These tangible actions will work alongside more advanced questions about ethics and uncertainty.

We’ll practice hands-on with de-identification and open-source tools such as QualCoder for qualitative data analysis and introduce some techniques that can be used. Participants are not expected to have any prior knowledge of these tools when coming into the workshop. There will be both case studies as well as opportunities to work on your project and receive feedback in the moment.

This session is great for qualitative researchers across all faculties, especially those working in Health Sciences, Social Sciences, and the Humanities. Whether you're new to qualitative methods or looking to deepen your approach, you'll find practical tools and insights to support your work.

By the end of this session, participants will be able to:

  1. Describe and contrast different qualitative data methodologies and be able to pick the most appropriate one for their project
  2. Prepare to record quality audio and develop a workflow for mixed methods data
  3. Apply some basic qualitative data analysis techniques using Taguette
  4. Experiment with de-identification, recording, and transcription
  5. Locate resources for data deposit and sharing of qualitative data and compare and contrast benefits and challenges
